$comment: Named periods a household recognises, mapped onto start years in the
historical record (see historicalReturns.json for the returns themselves).
WHAT AN EPISODE IS HERE: a retirement START YEAR, plus the name people use
for what happened around it. Picking one runs the ordinary cohort walk from
that year — it does not overlay the episode's years onto a different
retirement, and it makes no claim that this episode is the one that matters
to any particular plan. The severity ranking still answers that question.
EVERY EPISODE CARRIES ITS SOURCE. Dates that an authority publishes are
taken from that authority and nowhere else: NBER for business-cycle peaks
and troughs, FDIC for the savings-and-loan chronology, BLS for the price
record. Where a range is editorial rather than published — 'stagflation' is
a characterisation, not a dated event — the entry says so in `dateBasis`.
`anchorYear` is the year the RETIREE feels it, which is not always the year
the episode is named after; each entry says why it was anchored where it
was. Changing an anchor changes what the app shows a client, so the reason

nber.name: NBER — US Business Cycle Expansions and Contractions

bls-cpi.name: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Consumer Price Index

series.name: The bundled returns record itself — see historicalReturns.json

episodes.name: The Crash and the Depression
episodes.anchorReason: The contraction's peak month falls in 1929, so a household retiring that year meets it immediately.
episodes.blurb: Retiring the year the market broke, into the longest contraction in the record and years of falling prices.

episodes.name: The 1937 recession
episodes.anchorReason: The peak month is in 1937 and the whole contraction is short, so the start year is the episode.
episodes.blurb: A second downturn before the first recovery had finished — the part of the thirties most plans forget to imagine.

episodes.name: Post-war inflation
episodes.anchorReason: Anchored where the price record turns sharply after wartime controls ended; the range is a characterisation of that stretch, not a dated event.
episodes.blurb: Prices climbed hard while markets went nowhere — the combination that empties a portfolio without a crash to point at.

episodes.name: Stagflation
episodes.anchorReason: A characterisation of a long stretch rather than a dated event; anchored at its usual opening year so the whole of it falls inside the run.
episodes.blurb: A long stretch where prices climbed and real returns did not. Withdrawal plans are broken by this shape more often than by a crash.

episodes.name: The oil shock
episodes.anchorReason: The contraction's peak month falls in 1973. The sharp version of the stagflation era, for a household that wants the acute case rather than the long one.
episodes.blurb: The steepest part of the stagflation years, met in the first two years of a retirement.

episodes.name: Black Monday
episodes.anchorReason: A single-day fall with no recession beside it, so the year of the fall is the only sensible anchor.
episodes.blurb: A violent fall and a fast recovery — worth walking precisely because it frightened people far more than it cost a patient retiree.

episodes.name: The savings & loan crisis
episodes.anchorReason: The thrift failures span the eighties, but what reaches a retirement plan is the recession and bear market at the turn of the decade — so the walk starts there, and the name keeps the longer range.
episodes.blurb: A banking crisis rather than a market one. What a plan actually meets is the recession at the end of it: this walk shows the returns and prices a retiree lived through, not the thrift failures themselves.

episodes.name: Dot-com
episodes.anchorReason: Anchored at the market's turn rather than the recession's peak month the following year, because the losing years are what a retiree draws against.
episodes.blurb: Losing years stacked at the very start of a retirement — the sequence-of-returns case, in the form clients remember.

episodes.name: The financial crisis
episodes.anchorReason: The contraction's peak month falls in late 2007, but 2008 is the year a household saw its balance halve, and the year they name.
episodes.blurb: The one clients ask about without being prompted.

episodes.name: COVID
episodes.anchorReason: Peak and trough both fall in 2020 — the shortest contraction in the record.
episodes.blurb: A steep fall and an unusually quick recovery, both inside one year.

episodes.name: The inflation shock
episodes.anchorReason: No recession is dated here; the episode is a price and market year, so it is anchored on that year.
episodes.blurb: Stocks and bonds fell together while prices rose — the year the usual hedge stopped hedging.
